messages.subject_clean: Two postdoc positions for population modellers
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we have  two open postdoc positions which offer excellent career opportunities for ambitious population modelers. We are looking for candidates with a background in quantitative ecology, statistics, data science, applied mathematics or a related field. Both postdocs are fully funded by the Swiss NSF. They are originally for two years, but extensions are possible. In the first postdoc position, the successful candidate will model territory occupancy data to learn about dispersal and demography in raptors and owls. In the second postdoc position, my collaborator Trevor Hefley and I are looking for a candidate to develop ecological diffusion models to learn about dispersal and demography in bird populations distributed in continuous space, using ornitho/eBird-type of citizen-science data.

Both postdocs will work in the Population Biology group of Michael Schaub and myself at the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach, Switzerland. If you are interested please submit your application no later than 10 November 2022 here:  https://my.jobalino.ch/de/jobpreview/3705. You can drop me an email if you have questions. And thanks for distributing widely to people who you think may be interested and on any channel you deem suitable.

Best regards -- Marc

messages.subject: When to scale and centre interaction terms?
messages.subject_clean: When to scale and centre interaction terms?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

This may be a very novice question, but searching the internet hasn't provided an answer. I generally scale and centre my MSOM predictors (using base R's 'scale' function). When including interaction terms, when should I scale and centre? Should I (1) multiply raw predictors together to create a vector of interaction values, and then scale/centre these before modelling? Or (2) just scale/centre the separate predictors and combine them in the model itself without further changes? E.g.

# Option 1, scale and centre interaction before model.
Predictors$Area_by_Age <- Predictors$Area * Predictors$Age
Predictors <- scale(Predictors)

# Except from MSOM
logit(psi[i,k]) <- lpsi[k]
                                + betalpsi01[k] * Area[i]
                                + betalpsi02[k] * Age[i]
                                + betalpsi03[k] * Area_by_Age[i]

# Or Option 2, generate interaction within the model.
Predictors <- scale(Predictors)

logit(psi[i,k]) <- lpsi[k]
                                + betalpsi01[k] * Area[i]
                                + betalpsi02[k] * Age[i]
                                + betalpsi03[k] * Area[i] * Age[i]

I feel like Option 2 is probably the better route? I've tested these two approaches with a model I'm using, and get different parameter estimates, but the outputs from Option 2 look more like I would expect based on knowledge of species' ecology.

Many thanks,
Tom

messages.subject_clean: When to scale and centre interaction terms?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tom,

I find this a good question and had wondered about this myself some time ago, in the context of polynomial terms. I had then tried out different things like you and came away with the following impressions:
depending on whether you scale before or after forming interactions or polynomials, you will get different parameter estimates.
however, the predictions will be the same.
Therefore, it does not seem to matter; they are just different parameterizations of the same model. However, especially in MCMC algorithms, one parameterization may lead to better mixing than another, so that's something to keep in mind.

Corrections/comments welcome, as usual 🙂

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Thanks for your thoughts. It's reassuring to hear that they are the same model. Although when I try the two approaches I get different predicted species' median responses, not just different parameter estimates. Not just slightly different slopes, but in some cases a change from positive to negative response for the whole community. Moreover, this is for the linear predictors as well, not just the interaction terms. These are models with 100k iterations, 50k burn-in, and with all Rhats <1.1, so if they are just different parameterisations of the same model, they should give fairly consistent estimates? It makes me a bit concerned that there is something more fundamental wrong with my model if this small restructuring leads to such changes in the model predictions? While Option 2 (combination within the model) seems to give more 'realistic' predicted responses, selecting that parameterisation just because I prefer it doesn't seem like a legitimate approach!

Many thanks,
Tom

I don't think I know better but when standardization (or some other "innocent" change to a predictor) results in different results, one needs to check the parameter correlation matrix.  Such oddities can occur when two (or more) variables are highly correlated resulting in an overparametrized model.  I don't know if that's the case here but in any event the correlation matrix should be checked.  I wrote a function for doing so buried in the following thread:  https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/1WwomQMobCc/m/oRci9F1KAgAJ?utm_medium=email&utm_source=footer&pli=1.

Another thing I'd be curious about is the effective sample size of the parameter estimates.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The only caveat I would add to Marc's answer is that when using scaling (say z = (x-m)/s when m != 0) is that one needs to keep all lower order polynomial terms to guarantee equivalent models.  By that I mean the following:

When m != 0, then

    a0 + a1*x + a2*x^2

and

    b0 + b1*z + b2*x^2

are equivalent models.  But

    a0 + a2*x^2

and

    b0 + b2*z^2

are not equivalent models because the latter is (in terms of x)

    (b0 + b2*m^2/s^2) - (2*b2*m/s^2)*x + (b2/s^2)*x^2

So there is a linear term in x which a0 + a2*x^2 doesn't have.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Thanks a lot for all the input and ideas. I'm becoming more convinced that 'Option 2', (generating interactions by multiplying scaled linear terms within the model), is the right approach. 'Option 1' (generating interactions and then scaling) gives a lot of highly-correlated predictors (0.8 - 0.9), whereas 'Option 2' correlations are all <0.6 (and mostly much lower). So, following Jim's suggestion, maybe the Option 1 model is overfitted?

In response to the comments and suggestions:
- Jim, thanks for the link to the code to generate the parameter correlation matrix. Do you know how I could generate similar output from a jagsUI object, please?
- Ben, I think (hope!) my priors should be ok? I'm following Northrup & Gerber (2018), using logis(0,1) and unif(0,5) for hyperprior means and sds respectively. N.effs are ok in both models with no marked changes between them; all parameters have at least a minimum of low 100s, and there are no obvious 'bumpy' distributions in the parameter density plots.

However, taking the 'Option 2' approach throws up a complication when it comes to generating predictions. I follow the method in AHM chap 11:
- generate new data points spanning the range of the raw predictors,
- scale and centre the new data using the same values as used on the original predictors,
- extract predictions from the model,
- back transform predictions to standard values.

However, if I scale before generating interactions, there are no scale values to use on the new data versions of interactions. What would be the most appropriate to way to generate new interactions for predictions?  Multiply the new data scaled linear predictors together? In testing, this predicts much stronger curves for the interactions effects on occupancy, compared with predictions from the Option 1 model.

Thanks again,
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have a MSOM that gives improbably high estimates for the intercepts (0.999+ for all species). I wondered if it was something to do with my choice of priors, so I have tried a huge range of hyperpriors for the detectability and occupancy intercepts, from norm(0,0.01) to norm(0,1) and logistic(0,1). Nothing seems to make any difference. I have used the same model structure with the same set of predictors with other taxa using logistic(0,1) priors throughout, and the models run fine and produce realistic outputs.

The troublesome model has 89 species at 79 sites, with 2 - 4 visits per site. Structure is a standard MSOM, as per AHM1 chapter 11, but also includes a variance-covariance element to account for common species being more detectable (see attached). There are 16 occupancy slope parameters (10 linear, 6 interactions), and 2 detectability slope parameters. I run the model with 100k iterations, 50k adaptations and 50k burn-in. Rhats are ok, although n.effs are often small (~100 - 300). Detectability estimates are mostly very low, which I guess is then leading to the very high occupancy estimates.

Can anyone recommend a way to deal with this, please? Is there a combination of priors that will help? Or do I need to revisit the model structure? I would really prefer  not to change the structure, as I want to use the same for all taxa. But if I do have to think about that, what can I change that might help?

Many thanks,
Tom

Small sample sizes and few sites with observations, plus possibly small detection probs, which might lead to a positive bias in occupancy
Unfortunately, both proved to be wrong.

The data set has 89 species of moths surveyed in up to 4 occasions at 79 sites. The data are fairly "ecological" in the sense of being quite imbalanced: many sites have fewer than 4 surveys. Looking at the raw data did not show anything exceptional, and the observed proportion of occupied sites was reasonable. Here's a summary of that:

> summary(psiobs)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
0.01266 0.06329 0.10127 0.19414 0.25316 0.91139

The detection-nondetection matrix contains 17,000 non-missing entries, with 90% zeroes and 10% ones. I don't think this suggests extremely low detection probs.

Here are some of the things that I tried out:
Tom's original model had lots of covariates in occupancy and a couple in detection, plus an occupancy-detection correlation. I immediately discarded all that complexity and worked with an intercepts-only model without correlation. The problem of near-1 occupancy estimates persisted in this stripped-down model.
I then specified the priors for the mean hyperparameters for both occupancy and detection as U(0,1) on the probabilty scale, as in the following, but that did not help either.
  # Hyperpriors for occupancy
  # mu.lpsi ~ dnorm(0,0.01)   # Original prior on the logit intercept
  mu.lpsi <- logit(mean.psi)  # New prior on the probability-scale intercept
  mean.psi ~ dunif(0, 1)
Then I tried to implement the scale prior of Link (Ecology, 2013), which didn't work at all. (Although, to be honest, I am a little sceptic about whether I did that right.)

Dear all,

here's an interesting idea about the problem in Tom's model from Rahel Sollmann. She writes:

"one thing comes to mind (although I kind of doubt that that's the reason - see below): looking at the summary of species-specific estimates of p in the non-hierarchical suite of single-species models, the distribution of p-values looks pretty non-normal: the mean and median are <0.2 but the max is >0.7 (the skew persists on the logit scale). Maybe the normal hyperprior is to blame and a different distribution should be used? Have you looked at a histogram of detection probabilities - maybe their distribution is multi-modal? Results for psi are a lot more evenly spread between 0 and 1, that's why I am suspecting p to be the problem.

On the other hand, based on my own experiments with the Dirichlet process as a hyper-distribution (which allows for multiple modes), the regular Normal hyperdistirbution always worked just as well. That's why I don't think this is likely to be the issue. But easy to look at by plotting a histogram of p; and also easy to test by putting hierarchical structure on psi but keeping a fixed species effect on p. If that works ok, at least you'd know the issue is with the detection component of the model."

This is a question about whether the usual Gaussian assumptions about random effects are adequate or not (and there is some literature out there, both in the context of classical mixed models and also in the context of community occupancy models; see here:  https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/eap.2249).

However, here are 4 histograms of both parameters in Tom's analysis, on the probability and on the logit scale. In the two latter, I superimposed a normal density with mean and sd estimated from the species-level parameter estimates. I think these Gaussian approximations don't look fantastic, but I have definitely seen worse. So probably that's not the cause of the problem.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Meg,

I agree it would help to say more about your model.  The term state-space model can encompass quite a bit these days.

In a population dynamics state-space model, it is not uncommon for one of the variance components to have a maximum likelihood estimate of 0 (i.e. a precision of infinite).  Examples of where I think this has been discussed (IIRC!) include de Valpine and Hilborn (2005, https://doi.org/10.1139/f05-116, mea culpa for the self-ref), Knape (2008, https://doi.org/10.1890/08-0071.1) , and Auger-Méthe et al. (2016, https://www.nature.com/articles/srep26677).  It doesn't necessarily mean there is something wrong.  A confidence region around the MLE would still include non-zero variance values (i.e. meaningful, finite precision values).  But sometimes in a Bayesian context the choice of priors can really matter in these cases.  Some priors will lose reasonable coverage properties by allowing the posterior to have too much probability mass (possibly improperly) for enormous precision values, for example.

I hope that helps.

Perry
